briefs.brief: A developer has an AI agent that sometimes makes poor decisions, and the team has no dependable way to tell whether a change to it made things better or worse. They want a repeatable way to check how the agent behaves: scripted and simulated conversations, scoring of answers, comparing one version with another, and sometimes sitting down with business experts who judge the agent's answers so an automated scorer can be checked against them.

A developer's agent does not behave the way its written guidance to the model says it should: it ignores rules in that text, calls its helper functions too often or not at all, hands requests to the wrong helper agent, or crashes when placeholders in that text are filled from values saved during the conversation. Sometimes they are moving to a newer model and need to rework that guidance, or they want a few worked examples inside it and a way to keep it under version control with tests.

A developer's agent has to work with software running outside its own process: use functions offered by a separately running server through one of the open protocols that have become common for connecting models to external tool servers, call an agent another team runs elsewhere over the network, or make their own agent callable by other teams' systems. They need help choosing how to connect, wiring the connection up, and reviewing how it handles timeouts, filtering and versions.

A team's agent is live with real users and they cannot see what it is doing: traces are missing or doubled, they cannot work out what each conversation costs, nobody is told when quality or latency slips, and debugging one bad production conversation is guesswork. They may also need to hand day-to-day running over to a client's IT department or write up what went wrong after an incident.

A security-minded engineer looks at an agent that reads content from outside the company (emails, web pages, uploaded files) and is also able to take actions. They worry someone could hide commands in that content, that third-party tool servers it connects to could be tampered with, that the agent can do far more than it needs to, or that running code the model writes is dangerous. They want an attacker's-eye review and a set of tests that try to trick the agent.

A consultant or engineer is at the very beginning of an engagement: a business wants to 'do something with AI' but no particular project has been chosen, or there is only a vague area in mind. They need to work out where in the business it would actually help, which problem to tackle first, how success would be measured against today's numbers, and whether an AI agent is even the right tool compared with something simpler.

A developer working on an AI agent project built with Google's Agent Development Kit in Python has a broad or many-sided request: a change that touches several parts at once (for example the interface, the server, the agent's helper functions and hosting), or a request where they simply do not know which specialist area it falls under. They want a general starting point that works out which kinds of expertise the job needs.

A web application is built around an AI agent, with a Python FastAPI server in front of it. The developer needs work on the server's ordinary application side rather than the chat itself: endpoints for the app's own records (projects, invoices, uploaded files), making sure each signed-in user sees only their own rows, database migrations that sit next to the tables the agent framework creates, publishing the API description and a generated client, cross-origin and security headers, and how the server process is run in a container.

A developer is building the browser side of a chat with an AI agent: connecting the web page so replies appear word by word, showing what the agent is doing while it uses its helper functions, letting people return to and continue earlier chats, showing approve or reject prompts, coping with an error halfway through an answer, displaying small interactive panels next to the reply, or choosing between a hand-built JSON API and an existing open-source chat interface toolkit.

Before a client lets an AI agent go live, its lawyers, privacy officer and security team want paperwork. The engineer must work out which laws are likely to matter in the countries involved and then draft documents from what the project has recorded: an assessment of the system's effects on people, inputs for a privacy assessment, where data travels, a description of the system for reviewers, records of what personal data is handled, answers to a vendor security questionnaire and public-sector assurance forms, with anything uncertain flagged for a lawyer.

A developer's agent needs to remember things or look things up: recall a user's details and past conversations across separate visits, answer questions from a company's own documents, or prepare a pile of scanned PDFs, spreadsheets and engineering drawings so they can be searched. They also need users to be able to ask for stored data to be deleted, data to expire, and one user's or one customer's data never to leak into another's answers.

A developer needs an agent to return data in a fixed machine-readable shape, but it sometimes answers with chatty text, wraps the data in markdown, or produces something that fails parsing. Separately or together, they must decide which Gemini model version and settings to use (how much reasoning, how much randomness), cope with a model version being retired, or switch to a backup model automatically when the main one is unavailable.

A developer's agent sometimes gets stuck calling the same thing again and again or takes far too many steps, and the bill grows. They want hard caps per request and per user, a spending allowance that winds the service down in stages when it runs out, and a point where a person must sign off on certain risky actions before they happen, with a lasting record of who approved what and the ability to continue afterwards.

An AI agent has been designed to run on Google Cloud with Google's agent framework. Stakeholders such as procurement or a CTO are nervous about depending on one vendor and want a written assessment, without changing the build: how hard it would be to move to AWS or Azure or to a different agent framework, which parts are worth keeping swappable, what the risks are, and a rough staged plan with relative effort.

An AI agent project has results and someone senior must now make a call: approve a pilot, go to production, or keep funding it. The engineer needs a slide outline whose claims are backed by the project's evidence, what to say, likely tough questions and a one-page memo. After launch they may instead need user guides, training, launch announcements, or a regular report to the sponsor on what the agent has delivered for its cost.

A team ships changes to a live AI agent regularly: wording of the guidance it gives the model, model versions, helper-function definitions and configuration. They want those versioned together, automatic quality checks in their build pipeline that block a bad change, gradual rollout to part of the traffic with the ability to undo everything together, a plan for when the model provider announces a version shutdown, and test sets that stay current with what real users ask.

A developer has an agent that lets business people ask questions in plain English about data in BigQuery and answers by writing database queries. Problems include wrong or invalid queries, too much table structure stuffed into the prompt, making sure only read-only queries ever run, keeping a set of approved query patterns, and setting up and cleaning up the identity and permissions the agent uses to reach the data.

An engineer is about to build a new AI agent application on Google Cloud, or substantially rework one, and the use case has already been chosen. They want to think through requirements and the overall architecture with someone before writing code, decide what a first small version can include given the time and people available and what comes after, or turn that design into a proposal or statement of work for a client.

An agent's helper functions reach other systems on behalf of the signed-in person, for example their Google Drive or a third-party SaaS account. The developer must make sure each call acts as the right person and never another user, handle consent, token refresh and disconnection, keep API keys in a proper secret store, avoid downloaded service-account key files, and stop credentials from showing up in the agent's recorded history.

The functions an AI agent can call are poorly understood by the model: it picks the wrong one or passes the wrong arguments, there are too many of them, what they return is huge and crowds out everything else, and their error messages do not help the model recover. The developer wants to rework names, docstrings and parameters, merge or split functions, load only some of them at a time, or decide how a helper agent should be offered to the main one.

An AI agent is built from several steps or helper agents. The developer must decide how the steps are arranged (one after another, side by side, repeated until a condition holds, branching) or whether plain code would do, or fix what breaks where one step hands its results to the next through values saved in the conversation, or where hooks that run around model calls misbehave.

A developer's agent, built with Google's Python agent framework, works on their laptop and now needs to be hosted on Google Cloud for the first time. They must choose between serverless containers, Google's managed hosting for agents and Kubernetes, set up the identity it runs as, package it, check it works in a browser after release, recover from a failed rollout, and delete everything they created once a trial is over.

A hosted AI agent on Google Cloud is slow or costly to run: a long wait before the first word appears, slow cold starts, conversations getting slower as their history grows, poor use of each instance, or Kubernetes scaling that lags behind traffic. The developer wants to measure where the time and money go and make changes that are shown to help.

An AI consultant who works across many client engagements wants to keep a personal record of each employer's or client's background (their business and targets, regulations, stakeholders, the kinds of data they hold, their systems, tech stack and policies) and the lessons learned on earlier projects, stored outside any code repository so their assistant can reuse it on later projects. They want to set it up by answering questions or by importing their own documents, and to review, update or export it.

People paste personal details (names, card numbers, health information) or passwords into an AI agent's chat, and that data ends up in what is sent to the model, in calls to helper functions, in saved history, in logs and in the streamed reply. The developer wants to detect and mask it, screen what goes into and comes out of the model with Google Cloud's content-screening services, and plan the cloud setup those need.

An AI agent's helper functions call unreliable external HTTP services such as payments or bookings. The developer faces timeouts, uncertainty about when to retry, writes that may have happened twice (a double charge), and needs any action a user has approved to run exactly once and any declined action never to run at all.
